I mean, I guess I can hold it back for a minute if I really try, but it's hard. Like when I bought my TV, the cashier would not stop pushing the three-year protection plan on me. I just wanted to pay and leave, you know? But yeah, no, I don't do any of those weird behaviors to stop bad things from happening. It just happens.\n\nDoctor: If you try to hold back the behavior once it starts, can you suppress it for a short while?\n\nPatient: I mean, I guess I can hold it back for a minute if I really try, but it's hard. Like, if I'm at work and I start lining up the receipts across the floor, and my boss walks by, I can stop for a second. But it's just... I don't know why I'm even doing it. It doesn't make sense. Like standing by the copier with my hands up in the air until someone asks if I'm okay... I can put my hands down if I really focus, but then I just feel weird. \n\nSpeaking of the copier, our office just got a new one and it is incredibly confusing. It has this huge touchscreen menu that looks like an iPad, but none of the buttons do what you think they're going to do. I tried to scan a double-sided document yesterday and it ended up emailing it to the entire accounting department. Which was so embarrassing because it was just a lunch menu for that new Thai place down the street. Have you tried Thai food? I love Pad Thai, but only if they don't put too many peanuts on it. Some places just drown it in peanuts and then that's all you can taste. My friend Sarah is actually deathly allergic to peanuts. Like, she has to carry an EpiPen everywhere she goes. We went to a baseball game once and she couldn't even sit in our section because people were eating peanuts a few rows down. It must be so stressful to live like that, always worrying about what's in your food. But anyway, yeah, I can suppress the weird stuff for a little bit, like the calculator tapping... I tap it in sets of nine... but it always comes back.\n\nDoctor: When you do these behaviors, are they usually the same exact movement or pattern each time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure if it's the exact same movement every time. I mean, I don't really pay that close attention to it. Like with the receipts, I just line them up, but I don't know if I use my left hand first or if I space them exactly the same way. It's not like a choreographed dance or anything. \n\nSpeaking of dances, my sister is a dance teacher, and she's trying to put together this recital for her little kids, the five-year-olds. She's been complaining non-stop because they just run around the studio and won't stand on their little tape marks. She uses this bright pink gaffer tape on the floor so they know where to stand. Gaffer tape is actually super strong, it's way better than duct tape. I used some to fix the bumper on my car after that time I backed into a light pole at the grocery store. It was raining so hard I couldn't see out the back window, and the backup camera was all blurry. Those cameras are useless in the rain anyway. But yeah, the tape held the bumper on for like six months before I finally got it fixed. The auto body guy laughed at me, but it saved me from having to pay my deductible right away. Deductibles are such a scam anyway, you pay for insurance every month and then you still have to pay when something happens? It makes no sense. But I don't know about the patterns, honestly. I don't think it's exactly the same every single time.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever make sudden movements or sounds that you can’t really control, like blinking, shoulder jerks, sniffing, or throat clearing?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really do anything like that. I don't have sudden jerks or make sounds I can't control. I mean, sometimes my throat gets dry, but I don't clear it constantly or anything. \n\nSpeaking of dry throats, the air conditioning in my office is always blasting. It's like an icebox in there, especially in the summer. Everyone brings space heaters to keep under their desks, which I'm pretty sure is a huge fire hazard. The building manager, this guy named Gary, he sends out these passive-aggressive emails every month about how space heaters are strictly prohibited, but no one listens to him. Gary is actually kind of a weird guy. He collects antique doorknobs. He showed me pictures of them once on his phone. He has like, hundreds of them mounted on these velvet boards in his basement. It's such a specific thing to collect, you know? My grandfather used to collect coins, which makes a lot more sense. He had this one silver dollar from the 1800s that he kept in a little plastic case. He said it was worth a lot of money, but when we tried to sell it after he passed away, the coin shop guy said it was a fake. Can you believe that? My poor grandpa probably got scammed at a flea market or something. People will fake anything these days. I saw a documentary about people faking vintage wine, printing out labels on their home computers and putting cheap wine in old bottles. It's crazy what people will do for money. But yeah, no, I don't have any sudden movements or blinking or anything like that.\n\nDoctor: When you do these behaviors, is it the same exact movement or routine each time?\n\nPatient: I mean, I guess it is kind of the same routine. Like I was saying, I came in because I've just started doing these things at work—and at school, too—that just don't make any sense. Like lining the receipts across the floor, or tapping the calculator in sets of nine. Always nine. Or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I'm okay. \n\nIt's so weird, right? Like, why would I do that? But speaking of school, I'm taking this accounting class at the community college right now, and the professor is just... he's so monotone. He sounds exactly like that guy from those old dry eye commercials, you know? Like, \"Bueller... Bueller...\" It's impossible to stay awake. And the seats in the lecture hall are those terrible plastic ones that are attached to the desk, so you can't even adjust them. My back always kills me after an hour. I actually tried bringing a little lumbar pillow last week, but I left it on the bus on the way home. The public transit in this city is a nightmare anyway. The buses are never on time. I waited 45 minutes in the freezing cold on Tuesday because two buses just drove right past me without stopping. They put up this new digital sign at the bus stop that's supposed to tell you when the next one is coming, but it just said \"Error 404\" the whole time. Like, how does a bus stop get a web error? It's ridiculous. But yeah, the behaviors... they are pretty much the same routines, like the sets of nine and the receipts.\n\nDoctor: When you do these behaviors, do they feel like repeated movements or routines that you just get stuck doing?\n\nPatient: I don't really know if I'd say I get stuck doing them. I mean, I guess I do it until it's done, right? Like the tapping, I just do the nine taps and then I stop. It's not like I'm trapped there forever. \n\nSpeaking of being trapped, did you know that in some older elevators, if the power goes out, the emergency brakes clamp down so hard you can actually feel the whole car shudder? I read this article about elevator mechanics the other day because my building's elevator has been making this awful grinding noise. It sounds like two pieces of sheet metal rubbing together. The maintenance guy, Steve—he’s the one who replaced Gary after the whole space heater incident—he says it's just the cables stretching because it's getting colder outside. Which doesn't even make sense because the elevator shaft is inside the building. Steve is always making excuses like that. Last month he said the water pressure was low because of a \"solar flare.\" A solar flare! I mean, I'm just a bookkeeper, I don't know much about plumbing, but I'm pretty sure the sun doesn't affect the pipes in a three-story apartment building. I actually started keeping a log of all the weird excuses Steve gives. I have it in a spreadsheet on my laptop. I use Excel for everything now. I even made a spreadsheet to track my grocery spending, but then the grocery store changed their layout and moved the cereal aisle, which completely ruined my system. I hate when they do that. You go in looking for Cheerios and end up in the pet food section. But yeah, no, I don't feel like I'm stuck doing the routines, I just do them and then move on to whatever else I'm supposed to be doing.\n\nDoctor: When you try to hold back these behaviors, can you suppress them for more than a few seconds or minutes?\n\nPatient: I mean, I don't really know. I've never actually tried to hold them back, so I couldn't tell you if I can suppress them or not. I just do them. \n\nWhy would I try to stop, you know? It's just part of my day. Kind of like how I always get my coffee from this one specific cart outside my office building. The guy who runs it, his name is Sal, he knows exactly how I like it—medium roast, splash of oat milk, no sugar. Sal's great. He used to be a jazz musician, actually. He plays the saxophone. He told me he used to tour all over Europe in the nineties. He said the coffee in Italy completely changed his life, which is why he started the cart. He has all these crazy stories about playing in these tiny, smoky underground clubs in Paris and Berlin. It sounds so glamorous, right? Way more glamorous than bookkeeping, that's for sure. I tried to learn an instrument once, back in high school. I picked the trumpet because I thought it looked cool, but my lips would just get so sore, and my mom said I sounded like a dying goose. So that didn't last long. I still have the trumpet, though. It's sitting in its case in the back of my closet, probably gathering dust. I should probably sell it or donate it to a school band or something. Instruments are so expensive, and there's probably some kid out there who really wants to learn how to play but can't afford one. But anyway, yeah, I've never really tried to hold back the tapping or the receipts, so I'm not sure how long I could stop it for if I tried.\n\nDoctor: When you do these behaviors, do you feel aware of yourself doing them, or do they seem to happen outside your control?\n\nPatient: I mean, I'm definitely aware I'm doing them. It's not like I'm blacking out or someone else is controlling my body. I know I'm standing there with my hands up by the copier, or tapping the calculator nine times, or putting the receipts all over the floor. I know I'm doing it. It's just... I don't know why I'm doing it. Like, it doesn't make any sense. \n\nWhich is really frustrating because usually everything I do makes sense. I'm a bookkeeper, you know? Everything has to balance. Every penny has to be accounted for. My boss, Mr. Henderson, he's a stickler for the details. He's this older guy, always wears these terrible sweater vests. Like, argyle sweater vests in the middle of July. I don't know how he doesn't sweat to death in the office, especially because the AC in our building is basically a suggestion. The vents just kind of rattle and blow out lukewarm air. It smells a little bit like old wet paper, too. I brought it up to Steve—the maintenance guy I told you about—and he said the smell was from the \"humidity inversion\" in the ductwork. Again with the made-up science! I swear he just strings words together to see if I'll believe him. I actually looked up humidity inversion on my phone while he was talking, and it's a real meteorological thing, but it happens in the atmosphere, not in the ceiling of a strip mall accounting firm. I should add that to my spreadsheet. \"Steve claims weather phenomenon happening inside office.\" It's just wild. But yeah, I'm aware I'm doing the things with the receipts and the copier, they just don't make sense to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever do these behaviors just to break rules or show defiance?\n\nPatient: No, no, it's not about breaking rules at all. I'm actually a really rule-abiding guy. Like I said, I'm a bookkeeper, so rules are kind of my whole life. The IRS has so many rules, and if you mess them up, the fines are crazy. But no, I don't do the things to be defiant. Like I told you when I first came in, I'm only here because I started doing all these things at work and school that just don't make any sense. The lining the receipts up across the floor, the tapping the calculator in sets of nine, standing by the copier with my hands up in the air until someone asks if I'm okay... I don't want to do them, and I'm definitely not trying to get in trouble. \n\nGetting in trouble at work is the worst, especially with Mr. Henderson. He gets this little vein that pops out on his forehead when he's mad. It's right above his left eyebrow, and it pulses. It's honestly a little distracting. One time, this guy David—he used to work in payroll—he accidentally shredded a whole stack of original W-2s instead of the copies. Mr. Henderson's vein was practically vibrating. David tried to tape them back together, which is just insane. You can't tape a shredded W-2 and send it to the government. They use those cross-cut shredders now, so it was basically confetti. David actually got fired over that. Now he works at a car dealership, I think. Selling used Hondas or something. Hondas are pretty reliable cars, though. My aunt had a Civic that lasted for like, three hundred thousand miles. The only reason it died was because she drove it into a flooded intersection during a storm. The water came right up over the hood. The fire department had to come get her out in a raft. She was so mad about her groceries in the trunk getting ruined. But yeah, no, I'm not trying to be defiant or break rules. I just do these weird things and I don't know why.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever perform the same repetitive movement over and over for several seconds or minutes, like rocking, hand-flapping, or body posturing?\n\nPatient: I mean, yeah, I guess so. Like I was saying before, that's the whole reason I'm here. I started doing all these weird things at work and school that just don't make any sense at all. Like standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air. I just stand there like that until someone comes by and asks if I'm okay. Or the calculator thing, where I have to tap it in sets of nine. And the receipts, lining them all up across the floor... \n\nIt's so annoying with the receipts because thermal paper fades so fast, you know? If you leave a receipt in your car on a hot day, it just turns completely black. Or if it's in your wallet too long, the ink just disappears and it's a blank piece of paper. I don't understand why they still use thermal printers. It seems like a terrible way to keep permanent records. My dad used to keep all his receipts in this old shoebox under his bed for taxes. It was a Nike box, from these running shoes he bought when he decided he was going to run a marathon. He never actually ran the marathon, though. He trained for like three weeks, pulled a hamstring, and gave up. He said running was bad for your knees anyway. He started swimming instead. He goes to the YMCA every morning at 5 AM. I don't know how anyone wakes up that early on purpose. The pool always smells so strongly of chlorine, it burns my eyes just walking into the building. But yeah, I do those things like the copier and the tapping and the receipts over and over, even though they don't make sense.\n\nDoctor: When you do these repetitive behaviors, are they usually done to break rules or show defiance?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Like I was saying a few minutes ago, no, it's not about breaking rules or being defiant at all. I actually hate breaking rules. Even really small ones, like jaywalking. I'll stand at a crosswalk at midnight when there are absolutely zero cars on the road, just waiting for the little white walking guy to light up. \n\nMy friend Tyler used to make fun of me for it all the time. He was always breaking rules, though. Back in high school, he actually got suspended for climbing up onto the roof of the gym just to get a frisbee. Which is so stupid when you think about it, because frisbees are like, what, maybe five dollars? You can literally get them at the dollar store now. They have that whole aisle of cheap plastic summer toys. I bought a squirt gun there once for my little cousin, and it leaked the second I put water in it. Just dripped straight out the bottom of the handle right onto my shoes. I guess you really get what you pay for with that kind of stuff. The plastic is probably terrible for the environment, too. But yeah, to answer your question again, I'm definitely not trying to be defiant or break any rules when I do the weird stuff at work.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you choose to do these behaviors, even a little bit?\n\nPatient: No, not at all. That's the whole problem, honestly. Like I said, I only came in here because I started doing all these things at work and school that just don't make any sense, and I don't feel like I'm choosing to do them. The lining the receipts up across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, standing by the copier with my hands up until someone asks if I'm okay... I don't want to do any of it. \n\nIt's actually really embarrassing, especially the copier thing. The copier is right next to the breakroom, so everyone walks past it when they go to get coffee. We just got one of those fancy Keurig machines, too. The ones where you can pick the exact ounce size for your cup. It's supposed to be a perk, but honestly, those little plastic pods are so bad for the earth. I saw a documentary once about how many of those K-cups end up in landfills, and it's millions. They just sit there for centuries because the plastic doesn't break down. It made me want to start composting, but I live in an apartment on the third floor, so I don't really have a yard for a compost bin. My neighbor has a little worm bin on her balcony, though. She says they eat all her vegetable scraps. I think worms are kind of gross, to be honest. They get all slimy when it rains. But yeah, I don't choose to do the weird behaviors. They just happen."
